name: Pantera Capital
title: RT by @PanteraCapital: Just wrapped Money20/20. My biggest takeaway as a VC: the two forces reshaping fintech right now are AI agents and stablecoins. @SirDigitalDan from @CoinflowLabs and I dug into both in our fireside. Some takeaways: * Where will value accrue? AI is collapsing the cost of cognition, and stablecoins the cost of settlement. This changes value accrual, when those inputs aren’t scarce. I’m expecting value to migrate to regulated trust, proprietary data, distribution, underlying physical assets, networks. * What does stablecoins as programmable money unlock? Funds and spending rules can execute together, letting a product enforce agent budgets or trigger conditional payouts with less coordination across banks, processors and operational teams. * Where is agent demand emerging? Dan pointed to compute, inference and data APIs, which agents need to complete tasks. I’m looking for infra on fraud, KYA, chargebacks, and merchant side ops to help proliferate agentic commerce usage. * Who carries agent liability? A purchase can comply with the spending rules and still be a mistake. Before delegating larger budgets, businesses will want audit trails, a way to dispute purchases and an agreement on who absorbs losses. * Where’s the distribution advantage? Local integrations and merchant relationships give providers access to existing payment volume. Stablecoins can improve settlement without changing how customers pay. (Coinflow connects cards, ACH and PIX this way.) * How do existing PSPs participate? A provider can earn a processing fee when a developer funds an agent by card, even if subsequent payments settle in stablecoins. (Coinflow powers card funding for Tempo’s MPP Credits.) Thanks for the week @money2020! Curious what others took away too!

name: Nige
title: RT by @nigescore: Astra Ultra did not cook sports-grade vision AI. Gave it a 30s football clip from our subnet private track. Frame-level events, JSON, annotated video. Ground truth and the published scoring rules only after it committed. 22 predictions. 17 real events. 15 inside the action windows. 7 extras. 2 misses. Precision 68.18%. Recall 88.24%. F1 76.92%. Our Bittensor eval, SN44: 0%. Matches after timing decay: 16.538 False positives: −20.300 GT weight: 25.600 score = max(0, (16.538 − 20.300) / 25.600) = 0 Three extra take-ons and two extra tackles were 14.6 penalty points. It also misread the late interception/clearance. Rare actions pay more when you hit them and tax you harder when you invent them. Perfect timestamps on the matches still would not have cleared that bill. This was one offline replay of the published scorer. Unchanged preds. Not live latency. Not a season. The point is simpler than the arithmetic. F1 is what you post. SN44 is what you get paid on. Real matches, messy cameras, hard negatives, and a 30-second clock are not the same sport as a nice 15s clip to aura farm on Twitter.

title: RT by @covenant_ai: Crucible, Templar's pre-training platform, has completed its first production end-to-end training runs. The latest trained an 8B model on 50.53B tokens across 48 distributed A100s, at an estimated $0.1202 per million tokens of GPU rental. The run reached 48.3% effective MFU. At AWS p4de Capacity Blocks pricing, a 48-A100 cluster operating at the literature-derived 65% compute ceiling comes to an estimated $0.1686 per million tokens. Crucible's measured $0.1202 was about 29% lower after its low-bandwidth overhead. The comparison excludes R2 storage and operations. The full writeup shows the method and accounting. title: In an AI compute short squeeze, everyone in the stack looks smart. That doesn’t tell you who earns durable long-term returns. You can be right on demand and still own the wrong businesses. Today we estimate that every incremental GW of data center capacity currently generates $40-50bn of revenue across the stack. Data centers are under-earning (~$2.2mn/MW) relative to the value they unlock at the token factory layer (~$40mn+/MW). Frontier models face real pricing pressure from open-source and the hyperscalers. A 40% token-price cut can push standalone inference near breakeven — while hyperscalers still make money on the hardware. The picture will look very different in 6–12 months. Energy capacity, tokens per watt, model-layer competition, and financing are all in motion. We built a dynamic tool to track how it plays out. This map will look different in 6-12 months. Four forces to watch: - Energy, the most acute bottleneck today - More tokens per watt from better hardware and software - Rising competition at the model layer - Financing all this capex So we open-sourced our model. Input your assumptions and watch how value shifts across the stack.
